name: Social corporatism
summary: Social corporatism is a system in which peak organisations of employers and labour bargain over wages and economic policy, with government as mediator or supporter, inside a market economy and a welfare state. Its defining sources stress negotiated consensus between recognised groups, collective agreements preferred to legislation, and avoidance of the open class conflict that marked the interwar years. It is the democratic variety of corporatism, opposed in kind to state corporatism.
scope: Social corporatism in the sense of Katzenstein's 'social' variant of democratic corporatism (Austria, Denmark, Norway; Sweden close), as Perraton and Iversen describe it: peak employer and union organisations bargaining wages under market economies and welfare states, with solidaristic aims. It excludes state corporatism (Fascist Italy, Estado Novo), liberal corporatism (Switzerland, the Netherlands) and the Catholic vocational-order programme of Quadragesimo Anno.

notes: Later pass under rules 7. The earlier answers rested on Wikipedia overviews and inference from Nordic and Austrian practice; 176 are nulled and seven re-sourced to Perraton, Iversen and the Austrian partnership accounts. Read but not cited, because they never name social corporatism or its alias: Schmitter on societal and state corporatism, Goetz on Nordic corporatism, nordics.info on Saltsjobaden. Themes searched: definition and subtypes, Nordic and Austrian wage bargaining, welfare states, the Austrian Parity Commission, the 1938 Saltsjobaden agreement. The defining sources describe an arrangement, not a programme, so they state no position on most themes (government and law, world, liberty, culture, ecology, technology). The record is thin on most dividing lines, so failing the uncertainty rule is the honest result.
